strengths: Substantial benchmark scope: 2,700 curated samples spanning real-world and game-world scenarios across 8 primary dimensions and 18 sub-dimensions, addressing gaps (multi-object interaction, rule-governed game edits) that prior benchmarks (SmartEdit, RISE, KRISBench) leave uncovered.

The dual-reference evaluation idea (combining textual reference with a ground-truth image reference for VLM judges) is well-motivated and clearly illustrated (Fig. 2); this is a sensible methodological contribution beyond text-only judging.

The paper is a strong Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: beyond the benchmark, it releases UniREdit-Data-100K with CoT reasoning annotations and demonstrates the data's utility by fine-tuning Bagel into UniREdit-Bagel, which shows clear in-domain gains (78.87 vs. 71.64 for GPT-4o) and strong out-of-distribution results on RISEBench (18.3% vs. 9.8% for the Bagel-Think baseline) and KRISBench.

The multi-scenario data synthesis pipeline is clearly described, with distinct strategies for real-world (text-then-image with VLM scaling) and game-world (programmatic generation ensuring logical/visual correctness) scenarios; game data correctness is guaranteed by Python programs, a strength for reliability.

Supplementary material provides a detailed, multi-stage filtering pipeline (deduplication, six-dimensional VLM quality filtering, and two-stage human inspection with eight annotators and correction interfaces), supporting data quality and reproducibility claims.
Comprehensive benchmarking of 12+ open- and closed-source models with both aggregate (Table 2) and per-category (Table 5) results, plus qualitative comparisons covering failure modes of competitors.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: GPT-4.1 is the VLM judge, while GPT-4o is also a evaluated baseline, and GPT-4o generated essentially all real-world benchmark images and textual references. The 'ground-truth' images are themselves synthetic model outputs, which risks (a) GPT-family self-preference bias and (b) systematically favoring generators stylistically similar to GPT-4o. No evidence is provided that the dual-reference judge correlates with human judgments.

The evaluation protocol is under-validated: the weighted score S_overall uses fixed coefficients (0.5/0.3/0.2) with no justification or sensitivity analysis, and no human-study agreement statistics (e.g., correlation of VLM scores with expert ratings on a subset) are reported — a significant gap for a benchmark whose central contribution is the reliability of its evaluation.

Train/test relatedness concern: UniREdit-Bagel is trained on UniREdit-Data-100K produced by the same synthesis pipeline and (for real-world data) the same generator (GPT-4o) as UniREditBench itself. The large in-domain margin (+7.2 over GPT-4o) may partly reflect stylistic/protocol alignment with the benchmark rather than genuine capability; the OOD results mitigate but do not fully resolve this.

Statistical rigor is limited: with only 150 samples per sub-dimension, no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across judge runs/seeds are reported; single-judge (GPT-4.1) scores with two-decimal precision overstate the measurement certainty.

Game-world scenarios are largely pixel-art/synthetic renders (Sokoban, Sudoku, Pacman), which are convenient for programmatic verification but may not transfer to photorealistic rule-based editing; the practical relevance of this axis could be better justified.

Missing limitations discussion in the main paper: biases of synthetic GT references, judge dependence on a single proprietary model, and the benchmark's coverage of text rendering/typography are not discussed; the 'Project Page' placeholder on page 1 suggests the release link is not yet finalized, weakening reproducibility claims.

Some experimental reporting gaps: hyperparameters for fair comparison are only coarsely described (e.g., 'official inference settings'), the lambda_text/lambda_img weights for UniREdit-Bagel training are unspecified, and Table 4 lacks entries for several baselines (noted as '-' for some KRISBench categories).
The dual-reference evaluation requires GT images, which exist only for synthetic data; this limits the benchmark's extensibility to real photographs, an important scope restriction not acknowledged.

strengths: The benchmark covers a genuinely broader space than prior reasoning-editing benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench, SmartEdit): 2,700 samples across real-world multi-object interactions and rule-governed game-world scenarios, organized into a clear scenario-to-category hierarchy with 8 primary dimensions and 18 sub-dimensions.

The dual-reference evaluation idea (providing both a textual reference and a ground-truth reference image to the VLM judge) is sensible and well-motivated; the motivating example in Fig. 2 (text-only judge inflating a score for an image with an extra faulty path) is convincing.

Game-world data generation via Python programs is a strength: instructions, GT edits, and CoT traces in Sudoku, Sokoban, Pacman, etc. are programmatically verifiable, giving inherently correct supervision rather than VLM-generated labels.

Extensive benchmarking of 4 closed-source and 6 open-source models, plus out-of-distribution evaluation on RISEBench and KRISBench, provides a useful snapshot of the field; the finding that most models score below 60 on game scenarios is an actionable insight.

The supplementary material describes a concrete multi-stage data filtering pipeline (deduplication, six-dimension quality filtering, two-stage human inspection with 8 annotators), which supports data quality claims.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/bias in the benchmark: real-world images, GT reference images, and instructions are largely synthesized by GPT-4o, which is also one of the evaluated baseline models. Evaluating GPT-4o on data generated by itself (where it scores worst overall) raises questions about distributional bias, and all 'ground truth' references inherit the artifacts and failure modes of a single generator. No experiment probes this sensitivity (e.g., GT references from a different generator or human-created edits).

The central methodological claim — that dual-reference evaluation is 'more reliable' — is supported only by a single anecdotal example (Fig. 2). There is no human-agreement study validating that GPT-4.1 with dual references correlates better with human judgments than text-only evaluation. For a benchmark paper whose main contribution is evaluation reliability, this validation is essential and missing.

No ablation studies for UniREdit-Bagel: the contributions of CoT text supervision vs. image supervision, the dataset scale, the loss weighting λ_text/λ_img, or training on real-world vs. game-world subsets are all unexamined. The large in-domain gains over Bagel-Think cannot be attributed to a specific component.

Gains on in-domain game-world scenarios are hard to interpret as general reasoning improvement: game data is programmatically generated from a small set of hand-designed game templates, so fine-tuning largely teaches the model the template distribution. The +17 points over GPT-4o in-domain versus much smaller OOD gains (and Bagel-Think already non-trivial) suggest possible in-distribution memorization rather than reasoning transfer; a held-out-game analysis would clarify this.

The weighted scoring scheme (α1=0.5, α2=0.3, α3=0.2) is arbitrary and unjustified; no sensitivity analysis is given, and all three criteria are scored by the same judge (GPT-4.1), so correlated errors are unquantified.

Reproducibility is undermined: the title page contains an empty 'Project Page:' placeholder, and no commitment to releasing code, prompts, or the trained model is made in the text; for a benchmark/dataset paper, public release of the benchmark, synthesis pipeline, and evaluator prompts is a core requirement.

No human evaluation of model outputs is reported; all conclusions rest entirely on a single VLM judge, which is known to have systematic biases (e.g., favoring models that produce cleaner images regardless of instruction correctness).

The limitations discussion is essentially absent — the supplementary contains only a generic ethical statement; issues such as synthetic-data biases, judge reliability, and game-template coverage are not acknowledged.

Writing/precision issues: many key numbers (e.g., '+17.08', '9.1 points', '5.0 points') and protocol details are stated without error bars or significance testing; Fig. 5's dataset statistics are described for UniREdit-Data-100K while the benchmark's own 150-samples-per-category construction is only briefly described, making the benchmark/100K split somewhat confusing.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely gap: existing reasoning-based image editing benchmarks (SmartEdit, RISE, KRIS) focus mainly on single-object attribute transformations and text-only reference evaluation. UniREditBench's extension to multi-object interactions and human-rule-governed game-world scenarios is a meaningful and well-motivated broadening of evaluation scope, clearly positioned against prior benchmarks in Table 1.

The proposed dual-reference evaluation (combining textual reference with a ground-truth GT image for VLM-based scoring) is a sensible and novel contribution to evaluation reliability, and Figure 2 provides an intuitive motivating example of how text-only judging can be misled.

The benchmark is substantial in scale and structure: 2,700 human-inspected samples across 8 primary dimensions and 18 sub-dimensions, with a documented multi-stage filtering pipeline (deduplication, six-dimensional quality filtering, and two-stage human inspection with eight annotators), which strengthens data reliability and reproducibility.

The work goes beyond benchmarking: UniREdit-Data-100K with CoT reasoning annotations, and fine-tuning Bagel into UniREdit-Bagel with a clear training objective (CoT text supervision plus flow-matching image loss), provides a reusable resource and a proof-of-concept that the data improves reasoning-based editing.

Evaluation evidence is reasonably comprehensive: in-domain results on UniREditBench, out-of-distribution generalization on RISEBench and KRISBench (where UniREdit-Bagel is the best open-source model), detailed per-category results in the supplementary, and extensive qualitative comparisons.

The benchmarking of many closed- and open-source models (GPT-4o, Nano Banana, Seedream, Wan2.5, Bagel-Think, Qwen-Image-Edit, etc.) yields useful community insights, e.g., that game-world scenarios remain challenging even for frontier models (only GPT-4o and Nano Banana exceed 60 average).
weaknesses: The evaluation itself relies entirely on GPT-4.1 as the judge, and the central claim that dual-reference evaluation is 'more reliable' is supported only by a qualitative example (Fig. 2). No human agreement study, no correlation analysis with human judgments, and no comparison of judge reliability with vs. without the GT reference are provided. This is a significant gap given that the dual-reference scheme is one of the two headline contributions.

Potential self-evaluation/self-training bias: UniREdit-Bagel is trained on UniREdit-Data-100K generated by the same synthesis pipeline (and the same underlying VLMs) as UniREditBench, then evaluated on UniREditBench. The large in-domain gains (+17.08 over GPT-4o on game scenarios) may partly reflect distribution matching rather than genuine reasoning improvement. The OOD results mitigate this concern but the in-domain numbers should be interpreted cautiously, and the paper does not discuss this circularity.

The weighted scoring scheme (alpha_1=0.5, alpha_2=0.3, alpha_3=0.2) appears arbitrary; no ablation or sensitivity analysis of the weights is given, nor justification for why instruction following should be exactly twice visual quality.

Game-world scenarios are entirely synthetic (Python-program-generated grids, pixel-art-like games), so conclusions about 'long-horizon planning' or 'strategic reasoning' in image editing may not transfer to natural-image editing; the relationship and overlap between the 2,700 benchmark samples and the 100K training samples (risk of leakage) is not explicitly clarified.

Several benchmark-design details are under-specified: how the 150 samples per category were sampled, inter-annotator agreement during human inspection, the cost/feasibility of the GT-reference requirement for future users, and whether GT images (synthesized by GPT-4o) can themselves contain artifacts that bias judging.

The contribution type is Datasets/Benchmarks, which is appropriate; under that framing the model fine-tuning is a useful validation but not a methodological novelty, and the training section lacks ablations (e.g., contribution of CoT text loss vs. image loss, effect of lambda_text/lambda_img).

Limitations are discussed only minimally (the ethical statement is generic); a dedicated discussion of benchmark limitations (VLM-judge dependence, synthetic-data distribution, potential contamination) would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Clear Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: a 2,700-sample benchmark covering 8 primary and 18 sub-dimensions spanning real-world and game-world reasoning editing, with a transparent taxonomy and per-dimension examples (Tab. 1, Figs. 3, 5).

The dual-reference (text + GT image) evaluation protocol is a well-motivated and novel evaluation contribution; the motivating example (Fig. 2) convincingly shows text-only evaluators misjudging reasoning edits, and the ablation (Fig. 7) empirically supports the design.

Evidence is appropriate for the contribution type: human-expert correlation study (MAE < 1 across three scoring axes), evaluator-robustness checks with an open-source VLM (Qwen3VL-32B, Tab. 8), weighting ablation (Tab. 5), extensive OOD evaluation on RISEBench and KRISBench, data-scaling analysis (Fig. 9), and game-data transferability ablation (Tab. 9).

The synthesis pipeline is well specified (text-then-image for real-world scenes, programmatic game generation with verified logic), and the supplementary details on deduplication, multi-stage quality filtering, and human inspection improve reproducibility and trust in data quality.

Large-scale CoT-annotated training set (100K) with a simple, clearly described fine-tuning recipe yields strong in-domain and OOD gains (Tabs. 2, 3, 6), and the benchmarking of 16+ open/closed models provides useful community insights, including the 'logical hallucination' failure mode analysis.
Thorough documentation of game rules and evaluation interfaces in the appendix supports faithful reimplementation and reuse of the benchmark.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between benchmark and training data: UniREdit-Data-100K and UniREditBench are generated by the same pipeline, and the same commercial VLMs (GPT-4o/Gemini) are used for data generation, filtering, GT-image creation, CoT annotation, and as the judge. The +17-point in-domain advantage of UniREdit-Bagel over GPT-4o could partly reflect stylistic or distributional alignment with the synthetic reference images rather than superior reasoning; the paper should explicitly state that the 2,700 benchmark samples are disjoint from training data and discuss this bias.

The dual-reference protocol may disadvantage models that produce valid but differently-styled edits, since the evaluator compares against a single GPT-4o-rendered GT image; the paper does not analyze score sensitivity to reference-image style or report inter-reference variability.

The weighting ablation (Tab. 5) shows negligible differences (0.8357–0.8408), so the claim that (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) is optimal is weakly supported; this does not undermine results but the presentation overstates the evidence.
The human study is small (six experts, 200 samples, four models) and MAE < 1 on a 1–5 scale is a modest reliability bar; no inter-annotator agreement or statistical significance is reported.

Real-world samples are entirely synthetic (generated by GPT-4o), so conclusions about models' 'real-life' physical reasoning may not transfer to edits on natural photographs; this limitation deserves explicit discussion.

Several presentation issues: Fig. 5(a) word clouds and Fig. 4(c) are cluttered and hard to read; Table 2's in-domain gains are highlighted before clarifying train/test disjointness; the project-page link in the abstract is empty, and no explicit release commitment for the benchmark/data/code is stated in the main text, which affects reproducibility.

strengths: The benchmark offers genuinely broad coverage of reasoning-based editing, with 2,700 curated samples spanning real-world (single/multi-object) and game-world scenarios across 8 primary and 18 sub-dimensions, which goes beyond prior reasoning-editing benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench) in scope, as summarized in Tab. 1.

The dual-reference (text + GT image) evaluation protocol is a sensible and well-motivated idea, and it is supported by an ablation (Fig. 7) and a human study (Tab. 4) showing lower MAE against expert scores compared with text-only or image-only references.

The multi-scenario synthesis pipeline is clearly described, with a reasonably detailed filtering process (deduplication, six-dimensional quality filtering, human inspection) documented in the appendix, plus web-interface screenshots for the human stages.

Extensive benchmarking of many closed- and open-source models, supplementary evaluation with a second open-source VLM judge (Qwen3VL-32B, Tab. 8), and OOD evaluations on RISEBench and KRISBench strengthen the empirical portion of the paper.
Ablations in the appendix (game-world data transferability, CoT role, data scaling 20K-100K, weighting scheme) show the authors attempted to validate design choices rather than assert them.
weaknesses: A serious train/test contamination concern undermines the headline results: UniREditBench and UniREdit-Data-100K are produced by the same synthesis pipeline (the paper itself states the pipeline 'generates UniREditBench ... and UniREdit-Data-100K'). Fine-tuning Bagel on data drawn from the same distribution as the benchmark and then claiming the best overall score (78.15 vs. GPT-4o's 73.39) largely reflects distribution matching rather than superior reasoning. The paper never explicitly states that benchmark samples are held out from training or how the split was enforced, and the +17 point 'game-world' gain (where game data is programmatically generated identically) is particularly suspect.

The dual-reference protocol has an under-acknowledged conceptual flaw: it presumes a unique correct output. In the motivating example (Fig. 2), the edited image draws a valid, rule-compliant maze path, yet is penalized (score 3) merely because it differs from the GT reference path. This risks systematically rewarding imitation of the reference generator (GPT-4o) over semantically valid alternatives, potentially biasing the benchmark toward models stylistically similar to the reference-image generator.

Heavy dependence on GPT-4.1 as judge with weights tuned on a very small human study (6 experts, 200 samples, 4 models); an MAE below 1 on a 1-5 scale is a weak reliability bar, and no inter-annotator agreement or statistical significance is reported. Additionally, OOD comparisons on RISEBench use GPT-4.1 rather than the benchmark's original evaluation protocol, so the reported numbers are not directly comparable to published results.

Game-world tasks are synthetic pixel-art grids generated by Python code; while interesting for rule-based reasoning, their ecological validity as 'image editing' tasks is questionable, and models trained on such structured data (as UniREdit-Bagel is) gain an unfair advantage over general editors evaluated zero-shot.

Reproducibility is weak: the 'Project Page' field is empty, and no clear commitment to releasing UniREditBench, UniREdit-Data-100K, or the UniREdit-Bagel model/weights is made anywhere in the manuscript. For a benchmark paper, public release is essentially a prerequisite for the claimed community value.

Presentation issues: Table 1 is self-serving in design; several claims ('meticulously curated', 'substantial improvements') are asserted without sufficient evidence in the main text; and the fine-tuning methodology section adds little technical novelty (standard NLL + flow-matching fine-tuning on synthetic CoT data).

The paper does not discuss limitations of its approach anywhere; the ethics statement is boilerplate. For a benchmark whose central claim is evaluation reliability, an honest discussion of judge bias, reference-based scoring pitfalls, and contamination risk is expected and missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing reasoning-based editing benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench) are dominated by single-object, real-world scenarios and text-only evaluation references. UniREditBench's coverage of multi-object interaction and rule-governed game-world scenarios (8 primary dimensions, 18 sub-dimensions, 2,700 samples) is a meaningful extension with clear positioning against prior work (Tab. 1).

The dual-reference (text + ground-truth image) evaluation idea is well-motivated, and the paper supports it with evidence rather than assertion: the Fig. 2 motivating example, a human-vs-VLM MAE study (Tab. 4), and an ablation over reference settings (Fig. 7) showing the dual-reference protocol yields the lowest disagreement with human experts.

The contribution set is appropriately scoped for a Datasets/Benchmarks paper: benchmark + automated multi-scenario synthesis pipeline + 100K CoT-annotated training set + a fine-tuned model (UniREdit-Bagel) that validates the data, plus thorough benchmarking of ~16 open- and closed-source models.

Out-of-distribution validation is included and reasonably convincing: UniREdit-Bagel achieves the best open-source results on RISEBench (Tab. 3) and beats several closed-source models on KRISBench (Tab. 6), mitigating the concern that gains are purely in-domain overfitting.

Ablations are substantive and go beyond the minimum: game-data transferability (Tab. 9), CoT quality/alignment (Tab. 10), data-scaling from 20K to 100K (Fig. 9), evaluator-robustness with Qwen3VL-32B (Tab. 8), and a 'Logical Hallucination' failure-mode analysis that demonstrates the benchmark's diagnostic value.

The training procedure (optimization, loss weights, schedule) and the game rules per category (Appendix L) are documented in enough detail to support reproducibility; data filtering (de-duplication, quality filtering, human inspection) is described concretely.
weaknesses: Potential train/test distribution overlap is under-addressed. UniREdit-Data-100K and UniREditBench come from the same synthesis pipeline, and both rely on the same generators (Gemini-2.5-Pro for text/CoT, GPT-4o for images). The very large in-domain gains (+17 on game scenarios, and near-saturated scores like 98.30 on Tic-tac-toe) may partly reflect distribution/style matching to GPT-4o-rendered game boards rather than genuine reasoning. The paper does not explicitly state whether the 2,700 benchmark samples are decontaminated from the 100K training set; this must be clarified.

The dual-reference protocol risks penalizing valid alternative solutions. In the Fig. 2 example, the edited image receives score 3 even though the path appears instruction-compliant and is penalized only for deviating from the GT image (a 'detour into a dead-end'). This biases the metric toward mimicking the reference rather than satisfying the instruction, which is a conceptual tension with the paper's own claim that instruction following is what matters. The paper should discuss when reference-image deviation is legitimately correct.

The human agreement study is thin for the central methodological claim: 200 samples, 6 experts, 4 models, and an MAE < 1 on a 1-5 scale is modest evidence. The weighting-parameter analysis in Tab. 5 shows differences of ~0.005 in Pearson r between (0.5,0.5,0.2) and the chosen (0.5,0.3,0.2); presenting this as justifying the specific weighting overstates weak statistical differentiation. No variance/significance analysis is provided for any comparison.

The evaluation depends on a single commercial judge (GPT-4.1) by default; the open-source-evaluator cross-check (Tab. 8) is reassuring, but correlation of trends is not the same as agreement on absolute scores, and VLM-judge bias toward 'reference-matching' answers could interact with the dual-reference design.

Game-world dimensions conflate reasoning with low-level rendering ability; models may fail Sudoku/Maze tasks because pixel-precise grid manipulation is hard for diffusion decoders, not because logical reasoning fails. The benchmark taxonomy would benefit from an error decomposition separating reasoning errors from rendering errors, which is not provided.

The Project Page field is empty, and there is no explicit statement on public release of the benchmark, data, and model code; for a benchmark paper, availability is central to impact and reproducibility.

Some reported comparisons are incomplete or mixed-protocol: several models lack Temporal results on KRISBench; RISEBench accuracy percentages vs. UniREditBench 1-5 scores make cross-benchmark interpretation harder without a unified discussion of evaluator differences.

Minor: the abstract/introduction claims of 'meticulously curated' and 'substantial improvements' are repeated without qualification, and Table 2's in-domain framing (own benchmark, own training distribution) should be more prominently caveated in the main results discussion.
